title: DC Circuits & Kirchhoff's Rules
summary: Resistors in series add ($R_{eq}=\sum R$); in parallel their reciprocals add ($1/R_{eq}=\sum 1/R$). A real battery has EMF and internal resistance, so terminal voltage is $V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$. Kirchhoff's junction and loop rules solve any circuit, and RC circuits charge/discharge with time constant $\tau = RC$. (University Physics Vol. 2, Ch. 10.)

concept_sections.heading: EMF and terminal voltage
concept_sections.explanation: A battery's EMF $\mathcal{E}$ is the voltage it would provide with no current flowing. Real batteries have a small internal resistance $r$, so under load the terminal voltage drops: $V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$. That is why headlights dim when you crank the starter.

concept_sections.heading: Resistors in series
concept_sections.explanation: Series resistors carry the same current and their voltages add, so resistances add: $R_{eq} = R_1 + R_2 + \cdots$. The equivalent resistance is larger than any single one. Voltage divides in proportion to each resistance.

concept_sections.heading: Resistors in parallel
concept_sections.explanation: Parallel resistors share the same voltage and their currents add, so reciprocals add: $\dfrac{1}{R_{eq}} = \dfrac{1}{R_1} + \dfrac{1}{R_2} + \cdots$. The equivalent resistance is smaller than the smallest branch — more paths mean easier flow.

concept_sections.heading: Kirchhoff's rules
concept_sections.explanation: For circuits you can't reduce by series/parallel, use Kirchhoff: the junction rule (currents in = currents out, charge conservation) and the loop rule (voltage changes around any loop sum to zero, energy conservation). Together they give enough equations to solve for every current.

concept_sections.heading: RC circuits
concept_sections.explanation: When a resistor charges a capacitor, the charge rises toward its final value with time constant $\tau = RC$. After one $\tau$ the capacitor reaches about 63% of full charge; after $\sim5\tau$ it is essentially done. Discharging follows the same exponential decay.

real_world_examples.title: Holiday light strings
real_world_examples.scenario: Old series strings go fully dark if one bulb fails; modern parallel ones don't.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: In series, one break stops the single current path. In parallel each bulb has its own path at the same voltage, so the rest stay lit — a direct series-vs-parallel comparison.

real_world_examples.title: Car battery under load
real_world_examples.scenario: Interior lights dim when you start the engine.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The starter draws a huge current $I$, so the drop $Ir$ across the battery's internal resistance is large and terminal voltage $V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$ sags momentarily.

real_world_examples.title: Camera flash charge-up
real_world_examples.scenario: A flash needs a second to 'recharge' between shots.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: A resistor charges the flash capacitor with time constant $\tau = RC$; you wait a few $\tau$ for it to reach full voltage before it can fire again.

problems.prompt: Resistors of $2$, $3$, and $5\ \Omega$ are in series. Find the equivalent resistance.
A $6\ \Omega$ and a $3\ \Omega$ resistor are in parallel. Find the equivalent resistance.
A $12$ V battery drives a $4\ \Omega$ resistor. Find the current.
A battery has EMF $12$ V and internal resistance $0.50\ \Omega$. It supplies $4.0$ A. Find the terminal voltage.
problems.hint: Subtract the internal-resistance drop from the EMF.

problems.prompt: Three $6\ \Omega$ resistors are in parallel. Find the equivalent resistance.
problems.hint: For $n$ equal resistors in parallel, $R_{eq} = R/n$.

problems.prompt: A $5\ \Omega$ resistor has $10$ V across it. Find the power dissipated.
A $4\ \Omega$ resistor is in series with a parallel pair of $6\ \Omega$ and $3\ \Omega$. A $12$ V battery drives the circuit. Find the total current.
problems.hint: Reduce the parallel section first, then add the series resistor.

problems.prompt: A $4\ \Omega$ and a $6\ \Omega$ resistor are in series across $20$ V. Find the voltage across the $6\ \Omega$ resistor.
problems.hint: Find the series current, then $V = IR$ across the one resistor (voltage divider).

problems.prompt: A $100\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor charges through a $1000\ \Omega$ resistor. Find the time constant, and roughly what fraction is charged after one time constant.
solution_steps: After one $\tau$ the charge is $1 - e^{-1} \approx 0.63$ of full.

problems.prompt: A $10\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor charged to $100$ V discharges through a $5000\ \Omega$ resistor. Find the initial discharge current.
solution_steps: At $t=0$ the full voltage is across the resistor: $I_0 = V/R$.
problems.hint: Initially the capacitor's full voltage drives the resistor: $I_0 = V/R$.
